content.text: Part 1 — Changing the SELinux Enforcement Mode
Part 3 — Adjusting SELinux Policy with Booleans
Part 4 — Investigating and Resolving SELinux Issues
Part 6 — Chapter Summary and Command Reference

By the end of this chapter, you should understand how SELinux protects a Linux server, how to manage its enforcement mode, how to correct file labels, how to adjust SELinux Booleans, and how to investigate access-denied problems.
Main idea: SELinux adds an extra layer of security that controls what programs are allowed to access.
Linux file permissions control who can access a file. SELinux adds another question: Is this particular program allowed to access this resource?

Imagine an office building. File permissions are like an employee's keycard. SELinux is like an additional security guard who checks whether the employee is allowed to enter a particular room for a particular purpose.
For example, Apache is a web server program. It needs access to website files, but it should not automatically be allowed to read every private file on the server.
SELinux uses security rules to limit what programs can do, even when a program has been compromised.
Apache normally serves website files from /var/www/html. SELinux policy allows the web server to access files with suitable web-content labels.
Apache or httpd — the web server program.
/var/www/html — the standard directory for website content.
SELinux policy — the rules that determine which actions are allowed.
label or context — security information attached to a file or process.
Remember: Linux permissions help control who can access a file; SELinux helps control how programs may access resources.

sections.title: 1.2 Why are normal Linux permissions not enough?

content.text: Main idea: A program can have ordinary file permissions and still need to be restricted by SELinux.
Suppose Apache runs under a dedicated account and has permission to read website files. If an attacker compromises Apache, the attacker may gain the ability to act through that program.
Without additional restrictions, the compromised program might try to access other files that its account can read. SELinux helps limit this damage by applying rules to the program itself.
SELinux is especially useful because a security problem in one application does not automatically give that application unrestricted access to other services' files.
A web server needs to read website files, but it should not read MariaDB's private database files merely because it is running on the same computer.
httpd_t — the SELinux type commonly associated with Apache processes.
mysqld_t — the type commonly associated with MariaDB processes.
mysqld_db_t — the type commonly associated with MariaDB database files.
httpd_sys_content_t — the type commonly used for content Apache is allowed to read.
The _t ending is a common clue that a name is an SELinux type.
Remember: SELinux limits a program's access according to security rules, not just ordinary file permissions.

sections.title: 1.3 DAC and MAC: what is the difference?

content.text: Main idea: Linux permissions and SELinux use two different approaches to control access.
The book introduces two security models:
Discretionary Access Control (DAC): ordinary Linux user, group, and other permissions. The file owner can generally decide how access is granted within the limits of the system.
Mandatory Access Control (MAC): access is controlled by system security policy, such as SELinux rules.
Think of DAC as the owner of a room deciding who receives a key. MAC is an additional building security policy that may still prevent someone from entering even if they have a key.
A file may have read permission for Apache's Linux account, but SELinux may still prevent Apache from reading it because its security label is unsuitable.
DAC — access control based on ownership and standard permissions.
MAC — access control based on mandatory security policy.
SELinux — a system that provides MAC controls in RHEL.
Remember: Ordinary permissions and SELinux are separate checks; both can affect whether access succeeds.
Main idea: SELinux can enforce its rules, report violations without blocking them, or be disabled.
Applies SELinux rules and blocks prohibited access.
Does not block access because of SELinux policy, but records violations.
SELinux is turned off; SELinux violations are not enforced or recorded.
Enforcing is the normal recommended operating mode. Permissive can help administrators investigate a problem because it records what SELinux would have denied without blocking the access.
Disabled mode is discouraged because it removes this additional protection.
getenforce — displays the current SELinux enforcement mode.
Enforcing — SELinux rules are currently being enforced.
The command is read-only; it does not change the mode.
Remember: Enforcing blocks prohibited access, permissive reports it, and disabled turns SELinux off.
Main idea: Use getenforce to find out which SELinux mode is active now.
Before changing SELinux settings, check its current state. This helps you understand whether SELinux is already enforcing rules or only recording violations.
If the output is Permissive, SELinux is active but is not blocking access based on its policy. If the output is Disabled, SELinux is disabled.
getenforce — the complete command that displays the current mode.
Remember: Always check the current mode before attempting to troubleshoot an SELinux problem.

sections.title: 1.6 Change the current mode with setenforce

content.text: Main idea: Use setenforce to switch between enforcing and permissive mode without rebooting.
The setenforce command changes the current enforcement mode. This is a temporary change: it does not by itself change the default mode stored in the configuration file.
Expected output from the second command:
sudo — runs the command with elevated privileges.
setenforce — changes the current SELinux mode.
The 0 and 1 values are short alternatives to the words Permissive and Enforcing.
Remember: setenforce changes the current mode; it does not make that choice the permanent boot-time default.
Main idea: Edit /etc/selinux/config to choose the SELinux mode used at boot.
There is a difference between changing the current mode and changing the system's configured default. The /etc/selinux/config file stores the default SELinux setting.
The system reads this file during boot. A change to this file does not immediately change the mode of a system that is already running.
To make permissive the configured default, change it to:
grep — searches text for a matching pattern.
^SELINUX — ^ means the beginning of a line, so the search finds lines beginning with SELINUX.
SELINUXTYPE=targeted — identifies the SELinux policy type; it is not the enforcement mode.
Remember: setenforce changes the running mode; SELINUX= in the configuration file sets the default for boot.
Main idea: SELINUXTYPE selects the SELinux policy type rather than the enforcement mode.
The configuration file can contain both SELINUX and SELINUXTYPE. These settings answer different questions.
SELINUX=enforcing says whether policy rules are enforced.
The book identifies targeted as the default policy in RHEL. It focuses protection on targeted processes, such as important system services.
targeted — the policy type commonly used by RHEL.
= — assigns a value to the setting.
Remember: SELINUX controls the mode; SELINUXTYPE controls which policy is used.
Main idea: Kernel parameters can affect the SELinux state during boot.
The book also explains that kernel parameters can specify SELinux behavior during startup. These parameters can override the settings in /etc/selinux/config.
The important examples from the book are:
These are boot parameters, not ordinary shell commands to run by themselves.
A kernel boot configuration containing enforcing=0 requests permissive mode during startup.
enforcing — controls whether SELinux policy is enforced.
selinux — controls whether SELinux is enabled.
Do not casually disable SELinux on a production server. If you are troubleshooting, use the narrowest safe method and return to enforcing mode when appropriate.
Remember: Boot parameters influence startup behavior and may override the configured default.

sections.title: 1.10 Guided exercise — Changing the SELinux Enforcement Mode

content.text: The book's guided exercise practices both persistent configuration and temporary mode changes.
Main idea: You must be able to change the configured default, reboot to apply it, and change the current mode separately.

The exercise uses a training machine called servera. You connect to it, become root, change the default to permissive, reboot, and confirm the result. Then you change the configured default back to enforcing and use setenforce to apply enforcing mode immediately.
Then change the configuration back to SELINUX=enforcing and run:
systemctl reboot — asks systemd to reboot the machine.
setenforce 1 — switches the running system to enforcing mode.
Remember: The exercise teaches you to distinguish the configured default from the mode currently in effect.
Main idea: An SELinux context is a security label that helps SELinux decide how a file or process may be used.
SELinux labels files, directories, processes, and other resources. The policy uses these labels to determine whether an action is permitted.
Think of the label as a category printed on a file folder. A program is allowed to use the folder only when the security rules permit that category of access.
The book describes context fields for user, role, type, and sensitivity. In RHEL's default targeted policy, the type field is especially important.
The output includes file names and SELinux labels. A typical web-content label contains:
httpd_sys_content_t — a type commonly used for web content readable by Apache.
Remember: SELinux contexts label resources, and the policy uses those labels to make access decisions.
Main idea: An SELinux context contains several fields, and each field provides a different kind of security information.
A context commonly looks like this:
It is divided by colon symbols (:). Each colon separates one field from the next.
object_r — the role field for this object.
In the targeted policy discussed in this chapter, the type field is the main field you will usually investigate when troubleshooting web-content access.
The output displays the file's SELinux context alongside its normal file information.
Remember: Contexts contain several fields, but the type is particularly important in the targeted policy.

sections.title: 2.3 Display contexts for files and processes

content.text: Main idea: Commands such as ls and ps can show SELinux labels when used with -Z.
You often need to compare the label of a file with the label of the program trying to access it. The -Z option exposes this information.
Example 3 — Display labels for Apache processes:
a and x — select a broad set of processes, including processes without a controlling terminal.
-C httpd — selects processes whose command name is httpd.
ls -Z — displays SELinux labels for files.
Remember: Use ls -Z to inspect file labels and ps with Z to inspect process labels.

sections.title: 2.4 How files receive their initial contexts

content.text: Main idea: New files normally receive a suitable SELinux context from their parent directory.
When you create a file inside a directory, Linux usually assigns a context appropriate to that location. This helps files receive labels expected by the applications that use them.
Problems can occur when a file is moved from one location to another. The moved file can keep its original context, even though its new directory expects a different one.
Copying can behave differently: a normal copy generally receives a context appropriate to the destination, while a copy that preserves metadata can preserve the original context.
A file created in /tmp normally receives a temporary-file context.
If you move that file into /var/www/html, it may retain a context unsuitable for web content.
touch — creates an empty file if needed.
ls -Z — shows the file's SELinux context.
mv — moves a file; moving does not necessarily correct its SELinux context.
Remember: Moving a file does not guarantee that its SELinux label becomes correct for its new location.

sections.title: 2.5 Why moving and copying files can cause problems

content.text: Main idea: A file may have normal Linux permissions but the wrong SELinux context for its destination.
Imagine moving a folder from a private office into a public reception area. The folder's original classification may no longer be appropriate for its new purpose.
SELinux labels work similarly. A file moved from /tmp or a user's home directory into a website directory can keep a label associated with its old location.
Apache may then refuse to serve the file, even when its ordinary read permissions look correct.
Inspect the label. If it still has a temporary-file type rather than the expected web-content type, that may explain the access problem.
ls -Z — displays the context so you can check it.
Remember: When an application cannot access a file, inspect the SELinux label instead of assuming ordinary permissions are the only cause.

sections.title: 2.6 The three commands used to change contexts

content.text: Main idea: semanage fcontext, restorecon, and chcon are related but serve different purposes.
The book introduces three commands for managing file contexts.
semanage fcontext — defines or changes the stored rules that describe which contexts files should receive.
restorecon — applies the context expected by the configured rules.
chcon — directly changes a file's current context.
For persistent administration, the preferred method in the book is to define the correct rule with semanage fcontext and then apply it with restorecon.
This asks the system to restore the file's context according to the configured rules.
sudo — runs the command with elevated privileges.
restorecon — restores the expected SELinux context.
-v — verbose output; shows information about the operation.
/var/www/html/index.html — the file being checked and relabeled if necessary.
Remember: Define the correct rule first when necessary, then use restorecon to apply it.

sections.title: 2.7 Why chcon is not the preferred permanent fix

content.text: Main idea: chcon changes a file's current label but does not create the persistent labeling rule.
The chcon command is useful for testing or experimenting with a context. However, the change is not stored as a rule in the SELinux file-context database.
If restorecon runs later, it can undo the manual label change. A full filesystem relabel can also restore the context expected by the policy.
For this reason, the book recommends semanage fcontext with restorecon when you need a lasting configuration.
The directory's type is changed to httpd_sys_content_t.
If the configured rule expects another type, restorecon can return the directory to that expected type.
ls -Zd — displays the context of the directory itself.
restorecon — restores the context expected by the rules.
Remember: chcon changes the current label; it does not replace a persistent file-context rule.
Main idea: semanage fcontext stores rules that describe the expected SELinux contexts for file paths.
The system needs to know which context belongs to which location. semanage fcontext lets an administrator add, remove, or list these rules.
The book explains these common options:
Specify the SELinux type when defining a rule.
The output lists configured file-context rules. It can be lengthy because the system has many rules.
sudo — provides the privileges needed for administration.
Remember: semanage fcontext defines the expected labels; restorecon applies them to files.
Main idea: The (/.*)? pattern lets a file-context rule match a directory and its contents.
The book uses regular expressions in file-context rules. You do not need to memorize every detail immediately, but you must understand the common pattern used in this chapter.
* means zero or more repetitions of the preceding pattern.
Parentheses group part of the pattern.
Single quotes keep the pattern together so the shell passes it as one argument.
Together, the pattern matches /custom itself and paths below it.
'/custom(/.*)?' — match the directory and its contents.
Remember: The quoted (/.*)? pattern allows the rule to cover a directory and the paths beneath it.

sections.title: 2.10 Configure a persistent context for a website directory

content.text: Main idea: To serve web content from a non-standard directory, define the correct context rule and apply it.
The book's guided exercise configures Apache to serve a website from /custom rather than the standard /var/www/html directory.
Changing Apache's document root is not enough. SELinux must also allow Apache to access files in the new location.
Example — Define the rule and apply it:
The exact context fields and output can differ by system.
semanage fcontext — adds the rule to the file-context database.
-R — processes the directory recursively, including its contents.
Remember: A non-standard website directory needs both the correct Apache configuration and a suitable SELinux context.

sections.title: 2.11 Guided exercise — Controlling SELinux File Contexts

content.text: Main idea: The exercise shows how to make Apache serve files from a directory outside the standard web root.
The book's exercise uses servera. It creates /custom, puts an index.html file inside it, and changes Apache's configuration to use /custom as its document root.
The web server starts, but the browser cannot access the page because the directory initially has an unsuitable SELinux context.
The solution is to define a persistent file-context rule and apply it.
After configuring Apache's document root, apply the SELinux rule:
| — passes that text to the next command.
tee — writes received text to a file.
index.html — the web page being served.
semanage fcontext and restorecon — configure and apply the required labels.
Remember: When the website configuration is correct but access still fails, investigate the file's SELinux context.
Main idea: An SELinux Boolean is a switch that enables or disables a specific part of SELinux policy.
SELinux policy contains many rules. Sometimes a service needs an additional, specific capability that is disabled by default.
Rather than disabling SELinux entirely or writing a new policy, an administrator may be able to enable a suitable Boolean.
Think of a Boolean as an extra permission switch on a control panel. Turning it on enables the behavior described by that switch; turning it off disables that behavior.
The book uses httpd_enable_homedirs, which controls whether Apache can access users' home directories for web publishing.
off — the setting is currently disabled.
--> — the output shows the value associated with the Boolean.
Remember: A Boolean changes a specific policy behavior without turning off SELinux as a whole.
Main idea: Use getsebool to check Boolean states and semanage boolean to inspect their descriptions and defaults.
Before changing a Boolean, identify the correct one and understand what it controls. The system may contain many Booleans, so searching for a related word can help.
Example 2 — Search for Booleans related to home directories:
The pipe (|) sends the output of getsebool to grep, which displays matching lines.
To show Booleans whose current state differs from their configured default, use:
grep home — show lines containing home.
-C — show local customizations where the current state differs from the default.
Remember: Find the correct Boolean and understand its purpose before changing it.
Main idea: setsebool changes a Boolean's active value.
A Boolean can allow a specific service behavior. For example, Apache may need permission to publish content from users' home directories.
The book's example uses httpd_enable_homedirs. Changing it to on permits the policy behavior associated with that Boolean.
sudo — provides the administrative privileges needed to change the setting.
Without the persistent option, the change is not guaranteed to survive a reboot.
Remember: setsebool NAME on enables a Boolean for the running system.
Main idea: Use setsebool -P to save a Boolean change so it remains in effect after a reboot.
A temporary change may solve the current problem, but the setting could return to its default after restarting the system.
The -P option tells setsebool to make the change persistent.
httpd_enable_homedirs (on , on) Allow httpd to enable homedirs
The two values represent the current state and the default state. In this example, both are on.
semanage boolean -l — lists the Boolean and its values.
| grep httpd_enable_homedirs — filters the output to the requested Boolean.
Remember: Use -P when the Boolean change must survive a reboot.
Main idea: SELinux documentation can explain what a Boolean controls and when it should be enabled.
Do not enable a Boolean merely because its name sounds relevant. First read its description and confirm that the behavior is appropriate for your server.
The book explains that SELinux policy documentation provides manual pages for services and their Booleans.
This searches manual-page descriptions for entries matching _selinux.
man — opens or searches manual-page documentation.
-k — searches manual-page names and short descriptions.
'_selinux' — the search term, enclosed in quotes.
_selinux — often appears in manual-page names related to SELinux policy for a service.
The book notes that the selinux-policy-doc package provides relevant SELinux policy documentation.
Remember: Read the documentation before enabling a Boolean, because each switch has a specific security effect.

sections.title: 3.6 Guided exercise — Allow Apache to publish home-directory content

content.text: Main idea: The exercise uses an SELinux Boolean to permit Apache to serve content from a user's home directory.
By default, Apache may be prevented from publishing content from users' home directories. The exercise configures Apache's user-directory feature and then changes the relevant SELinux Boolean.

First, the Apache configuration must allow the feature. Then the user's public_html directory and page must exist, and normal directory permissions must allow Apache to reach the content. Finally, SELinux must permit the behavior.
The page can then be tested at a URL like:
public_html — a directory used for a user's published web content in this exercise.
httpd_enable_homedirs — the Boolean controlling Apache's home-directory access.
~student — refers to the student user's home-directory web content in the URL format used by Apache.
This exercise is from the book's training environment. Use a controlled lab before changing production web-server access.
Remember: Apache configuration, Linux permissions, and SELinux policy must all allow the requested access.
Main idea: SELinux can deny an action when the security policy does not permit it.
Suppose Apache should display a website page, but the browser shows an access-denied error. Ordinary file permissions may appear correct, yet the request still fails.
One possible reason is that the file has the wrong SELinux context. Another possibility is that a required policy behavior is disabled by a Boolean.
Do not immediately disable SELinux. First determine whether the access should actually be allowed, and then identify the specific reason for the denial.
If Apache cannot serve the file, the command may return an HTTP 403 Forbidden response.
curl — makes a request to a web address and displays the response.
http://localhost/file3 — requests file3 from the web server on the same machine.
403 Forbidden — the server refused the request; this alone does not prove SELinux caused the problem.
Remember: An access-denied error is a clue, not a diagnosis; investigate the cause before changing security settings.
Main idea: Investigate an SELinux denial before changing labels, Booleans, or policy.
The book recommends a deliberate troubleshooting process:
Decide whether the requested access should be allowed at all.
Check whether the file has an incorrect SELinux context.
If appropriate, consider whether a Boolean should be changed.
If the evidence suggests a policy bug, follow the appropriate support process.
The common problem is an incorrect file context, especially after moving a file. In that case, restorecon may be the narrowest and most suitable fix.
Changing Booleans requires more care because it can permit additional behavior across a service.
Inspect the file's context before deciding what to change.
Remember: Confirm the cause first, then apply the smallest appropriate correction.
Main idea: SELinux logs contain evidence about which process attempted an action and why it was denied.
When SELinux denies an action, the audit log can record an event known as an AVC denial. AVC stands for Access Vector Cache.
The record may include the process, the target file, the requested action, and the source and target contexts. These details help you identify the mismatch.
This searches recent audit records for AVC messages.
-m AVC — filters for AVC message types.
-ts recent — limits the search to recent events.
sudo — provides access to audit information that may require elevated privileges.
An AVC denial is evidence of a policy restriction. It does not automatically mean SELinux is wrong; the denied action may be unsafe or unintended.
Remember: Read the denial details to identify the process, target, and action before choosing a fix.

sections.title: 4.4 Understand the source context and target context

content.text: Main idea: An SELinux denial often identifies both the process making the request and the resource it tried to access.
In an audit record, the source context describes the process that attempted the action. The target context describes the resource that the process tried to access.
For example, Apache may run with the source type httpd_t. If it tries to access a file labeled default_t, the policy may not permit the requested operation.
That mismatch can explain why a website fails even when ordinary permissions seem reasonable.
httpd_t — the process type associated with Apache.
default_t — a generic type that may be unsuitable for files Apache must serve.
Remember: Compare the process context and file context to understand why the policy may have denied access.
Main idea: The system message log may contain a summary of an SELinux denial and a reference for investigating it.
The book describes the setroubleshoot-server package, which listens for audit messages and sends a summary to /var/log/messages.
The summary can include a unique identifier for an incident. That identifier can be used with sealert to display a more detailed report.
Press Enter to search for the term. Press n to find the next match and q to quit.
less — displays a file one screen at a time.
/sealert — the slash begins a search within less.
n — moves to the next matching result.
The exact logging setup can vary. If the expected summary is absent, check the available audit logs and installed troubleshooting tools.
Remember: System logs can point you toward the detailed SELinux report for an incident.

sections.title: 4.6 Use sealert to inspect a denial

content.text: Main idea: sealert provides a readable report explaining an SELinux alert.
An audit record can contain many technical fields. sealert helps organize the information into a report that is easier to investigate.
The book shows using a unique identifier found in the log summary. It also shows analyzing the audit log file for multiple incidents.
Replace YOUR-ALERT-ID with the actual identifier from your system.
-l — looks up a particular alert by its identifier.
The report can show the source context, target context, affected object, and possible explanations.
Remember: Use sealert to understand an alert before deciding whether a context correction or another fix is appropriate.
Main idea: ausearch searches the audit log for events that match specified criteria.
The audit log can contain a large number of records. Rather than reading the entire file manually, ausearch lets you filter the information.
The book demonstrates searching for AVC messages and limiting the results to recent events.
sudo — runs the command with elevated privileges.
Use the output to identify the process, the file or other resource, and the operation that was denied.
Remember: ausearch helps locate the relevant audit evidence instead of forcing you to read every log entry.
Main idea: When the evidence confirms that a file has the wrong label, use the configured context rules to correct it.
The book demonstrates a file that was moved into Apache's web directory but retained an unsuitable context. The web server could not serve it.
The recommended approach is to ensure a correct file-context rule exists and then run restorecon.
If the expected rule already exists, this command can restore the file's correct context.
For a directory and its contents:
Do not use a generic label change without checking the expected policy. If the directory is non-standard, first define the appropriate persistent rule.
Remember: Correct a context according to the intended policy instead of granting broader access than necessary.

sections.title: 4.9 Should you generate a custom SELinux policy?

content.text: Main idea: Creating a custom policy is not the first solution to every SELinux denial.

Some troubleshooting reports may suggest generating a custom policy module. However, the book emphasizes checking whether the access is legitimate and whether the problem is simply an incorrect context.
A custom policy can grant additional permissions. If the actual problem is a mislabeled file, adding permissions may hide the mistake and weaken security.

First inspect the denial, verify the source and target contexts, and correct a labeling issue when that is the cause. Consider more advanced policy changes only when the evidence supports them and you understand their security impact.
If Apache cannot serve /custom/index.html because the file has default_t instead of the expected web-content type, fix the file-context rule rather than immediately generating a policy module.
default_t — the file's current type in this example.
httpd_sys_content_t — the intended type for read-only web content.
semanage fcontext — defines the persistent rule.
Remember: Do not create broader permissions to solve a problem that can be fixed by restoring the correct context.

sections.title: 4.10 Troubleshoot SELinux using the Web Console

content.text: Main idea: The RHEL Web Console can display SELinux alerts and help you investigate their details.
The book explains that, when Web Console is installed, its SELinux section can show the current policy information and detected access-control errors.
You can open an error to inspect its details and possible solutions. After correcting the cause, check whether the alert remains.
Review the suggested explanation and possible solution.
Correct the underlying issue and check the alerts again.
Web Console — a browser-based interface for administering a Linux system.
SELinux Policy — the interface section for SELinux information.
Access Control Errors — the area where detected access problems may be listed.
The exact interface depends on the installed Web Console version and configuration.
Remember: Web Console is another way to inspect SELinux problems; it does not replace understanding the underlying cause.

sections.title: 4.11 Guided exercise — Investigating and Resolving SELinux Issues

content.text: Main idea: The exercise teaches you to diagnose a denied web request using logs and correct the underlying file context.
The book's exercise prepares a problem with a web directory called /custom. When you try to open the website, Apache returns an access-denied error.

You inspect /var/log/messages for the alert identifier, use sealert to examine the incident, and use ausearch to find related audit records. The evidence identifies the Apache process and the file whose context is unsuitable.
After confirming that the file context is the problem, correct it:
Replace the placeholder alert ID with the actual value reported by your system.
less — reads the system message log.
semanage fcontext — defines the persistent labeling rule.
restorecon — applies the rule to the directory and its contents.
Remember: Diagnose the denial from the logs, identify the cause, fix the context, and test the website again.

sections.title: 5.1 What is the purpose of the final lab?

content.text: Main idea: The final lab combines SELinux troubleshooting skills to solve a real access-denied problem.
The book's final lab presents a web server that cannot deliver content while SELinux is enforcing. Your job is to inspect the problem and adjust the configuration correctly.
The lab is intended to check that you can recognize relevant log messages, investigate the SELinux denial, and make the appropriate configuration change.
The exact setup and task instructions belong to the book's training environment. On your own system, use equivalent paths and configuration only after checking what is actually installed.
Example — Start by checking the mode:
Then inspect the relevant web-server files and contexts:
If the web server uses a non-standard directory, inspect that directory instead.
getenforce — identifies the current SELinux mode.
/var/www/html — the standard web-content directory in the book's examples.
Remember: The final lab tests whether you can investigate and correct the cause rather than simply disabling SELinux.
Main idea: Use a repeatable sequence to investigate SELinux access problems.
When a service cannot access a file, follow this order:
Confirm the service should have access to the resource.
Check the service status and the normal file permissions.
Check the file's SELinux context with ls -Z.
Inspect recent SELinux denials with ausearch.
Use sealert when available to understand the incident.
If the context is wrong, define the correct rule when necessary and run restorecon.
If the behavior is controlled by a Boolean, check its purpose and current state before changing it.
Test the service again and confirm that the problem is resolved.
If evidence points to a context problem, review the matching semanage fcontext rule and use restorecon as appropriate.
getenforce — checks whether SELinux is enforcing.
ausearch -m AVC -ts recent — searches recent SELinux denial records.
Remember: Diagnose first, make the smallest appropriate change, and test the result.
Main idea: SELinux administration in this chapter is about controlling enforcement, assigning correct labels, adjusting policy switches, and investigating denials.
Enforcement mode: Determines whether SELinux blocks prohibited access or only reports violations.
File contexts: Give resources the labels used by SELinux policy.
Booleans: Enable or disable specific policy behaviors.
Troubleshooting: Uses logs and diagnostic tools to identify why an action was denied.
When a service fails, you should not immediately assume SELinux is the cause. Check the service, ordinary permissions, configuration, and logs as appropriate.
For an Apache access problem, you might check:
systemctl status httpd — checks the web-server service.
ausearch — looks for relevant audit records.
Remember: SELinux troubleshooting is a process of gathering evidence and correcting the specific cause.
Switch the current mode to permissive.
Switch the current mode to enforcing.
Display SELinux contexts for processes named httpd.
Restore the expected context of a file.
Directly change a file's current type.
List SELinux Booleans and their states.
Enable a Boolean for the running system.
List Boolean customizations that differ from defaults.
Display details for a particular alert.
Analyze the audit log for SELinux incidents.
Search manual-page descriptions for SELinux-related entries.
-Z — show SELinux context information with supported commands.
-t — specify the SELinux type in the relevant command.
-a — add a file-context rule with semanage fcontext, or analyze a log with sealert; the meaning depends on the command.
-l — list information with semanage, or look up a specific alert with sealert; the meaning depends on the command.
-P — make a Boolean change persistent with setsebool.
| — send the output of one command into another command.
> — redirect normal output to a file, replacing the file's existing contents.
: — separates fields inside an SELinux context.
* — in the file-context pattern, matches zero or more occurrences of the preceding pattern.
? — in the pattern (/.*)?, makes the grouped part optional.
Single quotes ('...') — keep the pattern together as one shell argument.
Check the mode → inspect the context → understand the policy → read the denial → apply the smallest correct fix.
That is the core skill of Chapter 5: use SELinux as an additional layer of protection, and learn to diagnose its decisions instead of disabling that protection whenever something fails.
